science.title: Human-induced pressures and environmental factors drive the distribution of neglected tropical disease Buruli ulcer
science.description: Understanding the spatial distribution of skin neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) is paramount for surveillance and control strategies, although little is known regarding their natural origin, ecology, and distribution. This study aims to determine how natural and anthropogenic factors affect local to global spatial distribution patterns of a major skin NTD, Buruli ulcer (BU), and its pathogen, Mycobacterium ulcerans (MU). Generalized linear modelling of 110 variables grouped into five categories (i.e., physical, edaphic/climatic, animal diversity, plant diversity, and socio-demographic/geographic) were used to estimate continental-scale patterns of both MU and BU cases in Africa. Spatial models allowed the production of BU and MU maps for tropical and subtropical zones worldwide. Natural factors and their interactions consistently influence MU and BU distributions in Africa, with these distributions also responding to anthropogenic factors such as invasive plant species, agriculture and other activities. BU case distribution was driven by sunlight radiation, especially UV-B seasonality. Our extrapolation maps provide a quantitative understanding of the potential distribution of this pathogen and associated BU disease burden. Our findings highlight the utility of a disease ecology perspective using large-scale spatial data for understanding drivers of skin NTDs. Complex interactions between natural and anthropogenic factors indicate that developing preventive and control measures is challenging. Particular attention is needed on the role of invasive plant species in the spread of these pathogens, and the complex influence of sun exposure on skin NTDs. The ecological forces shaping neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) remain largely unknown. Buruli ulcer, a debilitating skin NTD, offers a striking case to explore how climate, biodiversity, and human activities interact together to drive NTD emergence and spread. Why does its spatial distribution align with some tropical regions but not others? What factors explain its geographical distribution across the tropics? Our analyses reveal that disease patterns reflect unexpected drivers, from presence of invasive plant species to seasonal sun exposure, alongside agriculture development and other human pressures. Extrapolated globally, these patterns highlight potential disease hotspots across the intertropical zones, with potential extension outside the tropics. By exposing how natural and human-derived factors converge to shape disease distribution, our work underscores the need for disease ecological perspectives in public health and offers a framework to anticipate emerging NTD risks. Aliaga-Samanez et al. examine the spatial distribution of Buruli ulcer and its Mycobacterium ulcerans pathogen using physical, edaphic, climatic, animal and plant diversity, socio-demographic, and geographic factors. Their findings show that interacting natural and anthropogenic drivers shape disease patterns and complicate prevention and control strategies.

science.title: Scientists discover a quantum effect that could eliminate batteries
science.description: Researchers have discovered how microscopic imperfections and atomic vibrations can be used to control a powerful quantum effect in an advanced material. The effect can turn alternating electrical signals from the environment directly into the kind of current electronic devices need, without traditional components. As temperature changes, the signal can even flip direction, giving scientists a new way to tune device performance.

science.title: Impact of ammonia hydrates and thermal gradients on the early geodynamic evolution of Enceladus’s south polar ice shell
science.description: Enceladus, one of Saturn’s icy moons, exhibits active geology and compelling evidence for a subsurface ocean. The detection of ammonia in its plumes indicates that ammonia–water ice mixtures likely play a critical role in shaping its internal evolution by lowering the melting point of ice. However, the distinct thermodynamic properties of both ammonia monohydrate ($$\hbox {NH}_{3} \cdot \hbox {H}_{2}\hbox {O}$$) and ammonia dihydrate ($$\hbox {NH}_{3} \cdot \hbox {2H}_{2}\hbox {O}$$) have not been systematically evaluated in geophysical models. In this study, we present numerical geodynamic simulations that explore how each phase influences the thermal structure, onset of convection, and potential for thermodynamic conditions favorable for partial melting within Enceladus’s ice shell, under varying ice shell thicknesses, reference viscosity, and thermodynamic parameters. Our results show that both ammonia hydrates allow for the development of conditions conducive to localized melting and influence convective behavior under specific constraints. Additionally, the ammonia dihydrate system may sustain convective activity even at relatively high viscosities, allowing for the generation of localized partial melting. These findings highlight that ammonia hydrate phase composition might significantly influence geodynamic behavior and could contribute to conditions favorable for localized cryovolcanic resurfacing.
